cards.a: War declared June 1812; Treaty of Ghent signed December 1814; Battle of New Orleans fought January 1815, after the treaty was signed but before news reached America.
cards.n: The out-of-order sequence (treaty before the famous victory) is a common trap.

cards.q: Identify the Hartford Convention.
cards.a: An 1814-1815 meeting of New England Federalists who protested the War of 1812, proposed constitutional amendments limiting southern and western power, and discussed secession or a separate peace.
cards.n: It met just as news of New Orleans and peace arrived, making the delegates look disloyal.

cards.q: Explain how the Hartford Convention destroyed the Federalist Party.
cards.a: Its complaints and secession talk arrived at the exact moment of Jackson's victory at New Orleans and the peace treaty, so Federalists appeared unpatriotic and even treasonous. The party never won a national election again.
cards.n: Ironically Federalists used states-rights and nullification arguments they had long opposed.

cards.q: Define the Era of Good Feelings.
cards.a: The period roughly 1815-1825 under Monroe when the Federalist Party had collapsed and one-party rule created an appearance of political harmony, alongside surging nationalism after the War of 1812.
cards.n: The name is misleading: the Panic of 1819 and the Missouri crisis show deep sectional and economic conflict.

cards.q: Define Henry Clay's American System.
cards.a: A three-part nationalist economic program: a protective tariff to shield American manufacturing, a national bank to provide stable currency and credit, and federally funded internal improvements such as roads and canals.
cards.n: Southerners resisted the tariff and federally funded improvements, so it was only partly enacted.

cards.q: Identify the terms of the Missouri Compromise.
cards.a: Missouri entered as a slave state and Maine as a free state, keeping the Senate balanced, and slavery was banned in the rest of the Louisiana Territory north of latitude 36 degrees 30 minutes.
cards.n: The 36 30 line was later voided by Kansas-Nebraska (1854) and declared unconstitutional in Dred Scott (1857).

cards.q: Date the Missouri Compromise and the Panic that preceded it.
cards.a: Panic of 1819; Missouri Compromise 1820.

cards.q: Explain why Jefferson called the Missouri crisis a fire bell in the night.
cards.a: The debate exposed slavery as a permanent sectional dividing line that could break the Union. Jefferson saw that drawing a geographic line over slavery would define politics for generations rather than settle the question.
cards.n: Strong evidence for causation prompts tracing the long road to secession.

cards.q: State the Monroe Doctrine.
cards.a: Declared in 1823 that the Western Hemisphere was closed to further European colonization, that the U.S. would treat European intervention in the Americas as hostile, and that the U.S. would stay out of European affairs.
cards.h: → two rules, one for each hemisphere
cards.n: Britain's navy actually enforced it; the U.S. lacked the power to back it up in 1823.

cards.q: Date the Monroe Doctrine and the Adams-Onis Treaty.
cards.a: Adams-Onis Treaty (Florida ceded by Spain) 1819; Monroe Doctrine 1823.

cards.q: Define the Market Revolution.
cards.a: The early 1800s shift from local subsistence and barter economies to interconnected regional markets, driven by new transportation, factory production, wage labor, and cash crops grown for distant sale.
cards.h: → from what economy to what economy
cards.n: It made the North and West economically interdependent while the South specialized in cotton, deepening sectionalism.

cards.q: Identify the Erie Canal and its economic effect.
cards.a: Completed in 1825, the state-funded canal linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie, slashed shipping costs between the Midwest and New York City, made New York the nation's leading port, and triggered a canal-building boom.
cards.h: → what it linked, which city won

cards.q: Explain how the transportation revolution reshaped sectional alignments.
cards.a: Canals and then railroads ran east-west, tying western farms to northeastern cities and markets instead of shipping goods down the Mississippi to New Orleans. This bound the North and West together and left the South comparatively isolated.
cards.n: A strong causation point for why the West sided with the Union in 1861.

cards.q: Define the Lowell system.
cards.a: A Massachusetts textile model that recruited young unmarried farm women to live in supervised company boardinghouses and work in mechanized mills that combined spinning and weaving under one roof.
cards.n: Lowell women organized some of the earliest labor protests in the U.S., including the 1834 and 1836 turnouts.

cards.q: Contrast the early Lowell workforce with the mill workforce by the 1840s-1850s.
cards.a: Early mills relied on native-born farm daughters working temporarily under paternalistic supervision. By the 1840s falling wages and speedups drove them out, and Irish immigrant families, including men and children, took the jobs at lower pay.
cards.n: Good continuity-and-change evidence on the degradation of factory labor.

cards.q: Contrast Irish and German immigration in the 1840s-1850s.
cards.a: Irish, driven by the potato famine after 1845, who were mostly poor, Catholic, and settled in northeastern cities as laborers and domestic servants; and Germans, fleeing the failed revolutions of 1848 and land pressure, who often had some capital and moved to midwestern farms and cities.
cards.n: The class difference explains why anti-Irish hostility was sharper than anti-German hostility.

cards.q: Define nativism and name its main political expression in the 1850s.
cards.a: Hostility toward immigrants and preference for native-born Protestants, driven by fear of Catholic influence and wage competition. Its political vehicle was the American Party, or Know-Nothings, which demanded longer naturalization periods and bans on immigrant officeholding.
cards.n: Nativism recurs in Period 6 and Period 7; use it for continuity-across-time prompts.

cards.q: Explain how the cotton gin expanded slavery.
cards.a: Whitney's 1793 gin made short-staple cotton profitable across the Deep South by mechanizing seed removal. Planters spread cotton cultivation west into Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas, and demand for enslaved field labor rose sharply.
cards.n: The domestic slave trade moved roughly a million people from the Upper to the Deep South after 1808.

cards.q: Differentiate the international slave trade from the domestic slave trade after 1808.
cards.a: Congress banned importing enslaved people from abroad in 1808. The domestic trade then supplied Deep South cotton lands by selling roughly one million people from the Upper South southwest, breaking apart families within the United States rather than across the Atlantic.
cards.n: A key MIG theme item: the largest forced internal migration in U.S. history.

cards.q: Define the Second Great Awakening.
cards.a: A wave of Protestant revivalism from the 1790s through the 1830s that emphasized emotional conversion, free will, and the idea that individuals could achieve salvation and perfect society. Charles Grandison Finney was its leading preacher.
cards.n: The doctrine of human perfectibility is the direct engine of antebellum reform.

cards.q: Explain the link between the Second Great Awakening and antebellum reform movements.
cards.a: Revivalists taught that people freely chose salvation and could perfect themselves and society, so believers, especially women, turned religious enthusiasm into organized campaigns against alcohol, slavery, illiteracy, and mistreatment of prisoners and the mentally ill.
cards.n: The single most reliable causation link in Period 4.

cards.q: Contrast the moral and the economic arguments for temperance.
cards.a: Moral reformers, drawing on the Second Great Awakening and led by groups such as the American Temperance Society founded in 1826, blamed drink for sin, poverty, and domestic violence. Employers backed temperance for practical reasons: sober workers meant fewer accidents and steadier factory output.
cards.n: Nativists tied drinking to Irish and German immigrants, entangling temperance with anti-immigrant politics.

cards.q: Identify William Lloyd Garrison and The Liberator.
cards.a: Garrison began publishing The Liberator in 1831, demanding immediate and uncompensated emancipation with no colonization, condemning the Constitution as a proslavery document, and founding the American Anti-Slavery Society in 1833.
cards.n: Immediatism marked a sharp break from earlier gradual emancipation and colonization schemes.

cards.q: Identify Frederick Douglass and his contribution to abolition.
cards.a: An escaped enslaved man who became the movement's most powerful speaker, published the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass in 1845, and founded the North Star in 1847, arguing that the Constitution could be used as an antislavery weapon.
cards.n: His split with Garrison over the Constitution and political action is a classic comparison question.

cards.q: Identify David Walker's Appeal.
cards.a: Walker's Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World (1829) was a militant pamphlet by a free Black Bostonian that condemned slavery and racism and urged enslaved people to resist, by violence if necessary.
cards.n: Southern states banned it and blamed such writings for Nat Turner's 1831 rebellion.

cards.q: Contrast Garrison's and Douglass's strategies for ending slavery.
cards.a: Garrison rejected politics, burned the Constitution as a covenant with death, and urged moral suasion and northern disunion. Douglass came to argue that the Constitution was antislavery and that abolitionists should vote, organize parties, and use government power.
cards.h: → attitude toward the Constitution and voting
cards.n: Both are immediatists; the difference is means, not goals.

cards.q: Identify the Seneca Falls Convention.
cards.a: The first women's rights convention in the United States, held in New York in 1848 and organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. It issued the Declaration of Sentiments demanding legal equality and, most controversially, suffrage.
cards.n: Many attendees came out of abolitionism, where women were barred from speaking.

cards.q: State what the Declaration of Sentiments argued and what document it imitated.
cards.a: Modeled on the Declaration of Independence, it declared that all men and women are created equal and listed the injuries of men toward women, including denial of the vote, property rights, education, and legal standing in marriage.
cards.n: Using the Declaration's form was a deliberate rhetorical claim to the Revolution's legacy.

cards.q: Date the Seneca Falls Convention and the founding of the American Anti-Slavery Society and its female auxiliaries.
cards.a: American Anti-Slavery Society founded 1833 with women organizing female auxiliaries from 1833-1837; Seneca Falls Convention 1848.

cards.q: Identify Dorothea Dix and her reform campaign.
cards.a: A Massachusetts teacher who documented the confinement of the mentally ill in jails and almshouses and lobbied state legislatures from the 1840s to build publicly funded asylums offering treatment rather than punishment.
cards.n: Part of a broader shift toward state-run institutions, including penitentiaries designed to reform rather than merely punish.

cards.q: Identify Horace Mann and the common school movement.
cards.a: As Massachusetts secretary of education from 1837, Mann pushed for tax-supported public elementary schools, longer school years, standardized curricula, and teacher training in normal schools, arguing that education would make citizens and equalize opportunity.
cards.h: → what kind of school, funded how
cards.n: Teaching became a leading paid profession for women, which reformers justified as an extension of motherhood.

cards.q: Define utopian communities and name several examples.
cards.a: Experimental settlements that withdrew from mainstream society to model a perfected social order. Examples: the Shakers (celibacy and communal property), New Harmony (Owen's secular socialism), Oneida (complex marriage and communal child rearing), and Brook Farm (transcendentalist).

cards.q: Define transcendentalism.
cards.a: A New England intellectual movement led by Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau holding that truth comes from intuition and nature rather than from institutions or empirical reason, and celebrating self-reliance and individual conscience.
cards.n: Thoreau's Civil Disobedience, written against the Mexican-American War, later influenced Gandhi and King.

cards.q: Define the cult of domesticity.
cards.a: The middle-class ideal that emerged with the Market Revolution assigning women a separate private sphere of home, piety, purity, and child rearing, while men occupied the public world of work and politics.
cards.n: It applied mainly to white middle-class women; poor, immigrant, and enslaved women worked outside the home.

cards.q: Contrast the cult of domesticity with the women's rights movement of the 1840s.
cards.a: The cult of domesticity confined women to a moral private sphere; the women's rights movement demanded entry to the public sphere through suffrage, property rights, and legal standing. Yet reformers often used domesticity's claim of female moral superiority to justify public activism.
cards.n: The best answers note that domesticity both limited women and gave them a platform.

cards.q: Define Jacksonian democracy.
cards.a: The 1820s-1830s expansion of political participation through near-universal white male suffrage, popular election of presidential electors, nominating conventions, and rhetoric pitting the common man against entrenched elites and monopolies.
cards.h: → who gained the vote, who was excluded
cards.n: Expansion for white men coincided with the disfranchisement of free Black men in states like Pennsylvania and New York.

cards.q: Define the spoils system.
cards.a: Jackson's practice of replacing federal officeholders with loyal supporters, defended as rotation in office that prevented an entrenched bureaucracy and let ordinary citizens serve. Critics called it patronage that rewarded loyalty over competence.
cards.n: It is the target of civil service reform later, in the 1883 Pendleton Act.

cards.q: Identify the nullification crisis.
cards.a: South Carolina, guided by Calhoun's doctrine that a state could void federal law, declared the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 null in 1832. Jackson obtained a Force Bill authorizing military enforcement while Clay brokered a compromise tariff that lowered rates over ten years.
cards.h: → state, doctrine, and how it ended
cards.n: Jackson the states-rights Democrat defended federal supremacy here, which surprises students.

cards.q: Explain the long-term significance of the nullification crisis.
cards.a: It rehearsed the constitutional argument of secession: whether sovereignty rests with the states or the national government. Compromise deferred the fight, but South Carolina's willingness to defy federal law foreshadowed 1860.
cards.n: The tariff was the occasion; protecting slavery from federal power was the underlying stake.

cards.q: Identify the Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears.
cards.a: The 1830 act authorized the president to negotiate the exchange of eastern Native lands for territory west of the Mississippi. Enforcement drove the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole west; the Cherokee march of 1838-1839 killed roughly 4,000 and is called the Trail of Tears.
cards.n: The Cherokee had adopted a written constitution, alphabet, and farms, so removal was not about assimilation.

cards.q: Date the Indian Removal Act, Worcester v. Georgia, and the Cherokee Trail of Tears.
cards.a: Indian Removal Act 1830; Worcester v. Georgia 1832; Cherokee Trail of Tears 1838-1839.
cards.n: The Court ruled against removal two years after the act and six years before the march.

cards.q: Identify the Bank War.
cards.a: Jackson's campaign against the Second Bank of the United States: he vetoed its early recharter in 1832 as an unconstitutional monopoly serving the rich, won reelection on the issue, and then removed federal deposits into state pet banks.
cards.n: The veto message is a key document for Jacksonian rhetoric about privilege and the common man.

cards.q: Explain how Jackson's financial policies contributed to the Panic of 1837.
cards.a: Moving deposits to pet banks fueled easy credit and land speculation, and the 1836 Specie Circular then required payment for public land in gold or silver. Credit collapsed, banks failed, and a depression lasting into the 1840s fell on Van Buren.
cards.n: Whigs blamed executive tyranny; the depression helped elect Harrison in 1840.

cards.q: Contrast the Whigs and the Jacksonian Democrats.
cards.a: Whigs backed Clay's American System, a national bank, protective tariffs, internal improvements, and moral reform, drawing business and evangelical support. Democrats wanted limited government, no national bank, low tariffs, expansion, and strong executive power, drawing farmers, workers, and immigrants.
cards.n: Both parties were national coalitions that avoided slavery to survive, which is why both fractured in the 1850s.

cards.q: Differentiate the First Party System from the Second Party System.
cards.a: The First System pitted Federalists against Democratic-Republicans in an era of limited suffrage and elite politics. The Second System pitted Whigs against Democrats with near-universal white male suffrage, nominating conventions, and mass campaigning, as in the 1840 log cabin campaign with about 80 percent turnout.
cards.n: Whigs won in 1840 by copying Jacksonian mass techniques rather than by arguing policy.

cards.q: Define manifest destiny.
cards.a: The 1840s belief, named by John O'Sullivan in 1845, that God and destiny had chosen the United States to expand across North America and spread its institutions, used to justify annexing Texas, Oregon, and the Mexican Cession.
cards.n: It carried explicit racial assumptions about Anglo-Saxon superiority over Mexicans and Native peoples.

cards.q: Explain why Texas annexation was delayed nine years after independence.
cards.a: American settlers in Mexican Texas revolted and won independence at San Jacinto in 1836. Annexation stalled for nine years over the sectional balance and fear of war with Mexico, until Congress annexed Texas by joint resolution in 1845 after Polk's election.
cards.n: A joint resolution needed only simple majorities, bypassing the two-thirds treaty requirement in the Senate.

cards.q: Explain how and why the Oregon boundary dispute was settled short of war.
cards.a: Polk campaigned on Fifty-Four Forty or Fight but, facing war with Mexico, compromised with Britain in 1846 on the 49th parallel, dividing Oregon and giving the U.S. Puget Sound.
cards.n: Northerners noticed Polk fought Mexico for southern land while compromising on northern land.

cards.q: Explain how Polk brought on the Mexican-American War.
cards.a: Polk claimed the Rio Grande as the Texas border while Mexico claimed the Nueces River. He sent Taylor's troops into the disputed strip, and after a clash there in April 1846 he told Congress that Mexico had shed American blood on American soil.
cards.n: Whigs, including Lincoln with his Spot Resolutions, charged Polk with provoking the war.

cards.q: Identify the terms of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.
cards.a: The 1848 treaty ended the war, confirmed the Rio Grande border, and transferred California and the Southwest (the Mexican Cession) to the U.S. for $15 million and assumption of claims. Mexicans in the territory were promised citizenship and property rights.
cards.n: Those property guarantees were widely violated, a standard point for MIG and SOC questions.

cards.q: Date the annexation of Texas, the Mexican-American War, and the Gadsden Purchase.
cards.a: Texas annexed 1845; Mexican-American War 1846-1848; Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo 1848; Gadsden Purchase 1853.

cards.q: Explain why the Mexican Cession reopened the slavery question.
cards.a: The Missouri Compromise line covered only the Louisiana Purchase, so the new southwestern territory had no rule. Every proposal about slavery there forced a sectional vote, and the parties could no longer avoid the issue.
cards.h: → why the old line did not apply
cards.n: Emerson predicted the conquest would be poison; use this for causation prompts on the coming of the war.

cards.q: Identify the Wilmot Proviso and its fate.
cards.a: An 1846 amendment by Representative David Wilmot to bar slavery from any territory taken from Mexico. It passed the House repeatedly, where free states held a majority, but always died in the Senate, where the sections were balanced.
cards.h: → what it proposed + where it died
cards.n: House-versus-Senate voting shows sectional alignment overriding party loyalty as early as 1846.

cards.q: Define popular sovereignty as applied to slavery in the territories.
cards.a: The doctrine, associated with Lewis Cass and Stephen Douglas, that settlers in a territory should vote to decide whether slavery would be permitted there, removing the question from Congress.
cards.n: It sounded democratic but caused violence in Kansas because it never specified when the vote should occur.

cards.q: Differentiate free soil from abolition.
cards.a: Abolitionists wanted slavery destroyed everywhere as a moral evil. Free soilers, organized in the 1848 Free Soil Party under free soil, free labor, free men, only opposed slavery's extension into the territories, largely to protect white farmers and workers from slave-labor competition.
cards.n: The Republican Party of 1854 is a free soil party, not an abolitionist one; the distinction is heavily tested.

cards.q: Identify the five provisions of the Compromise of 1850.
cards.a: California admitted free; the rest of the Mexican Cession organized as Utah and New Mexico with popular sovereignty; the Texas-New Mexico border adjusted with Texas debt assumed; the slave trade banned in Washington, D.C.; and a stringent new Fugitive Slave Act.
cards.n: Douglas passed it as separate bills after Clay's omnibus failed, so no member had to vote for all of it.

cards.q: Date the Wilmot Proviso, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act.
cards.a: Wilmot Proviso 1846; Compromise of 1850; Kansas-Nebraska Act 1854.

cards.q: Identify the provisions of the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850.
cards.a: It required federal commissioners to hear claims without a jury trial or testimony from the accused, paid commissioners more for ruling in favor of the claimant, and compelled northern citizens and officials to assist in captures under penalty of fine and imprisonment.
cards.n: The pay differential and denial of jury trial are the details graders reward.

cards.q: Explain why the Fugitive Slave Act radicalized northern opinion.
cards.a: It made ordinary northerners legally complicit in slavery rather than distant observers. Personal liberty laws, mob rescues of captured fugitives, and rising Underground Railroad activity followed, and many moderates moved toward antislavery politics.
cards.n: Ironically the slaveholders' greatest legislative win did the most to create a northern antislavery majority.

cards.q: Identify Uncle Tom's Cabin and its impact.
cards.a: Harriet Beecher Stowe's 1852 novel, written in reaction to the Fugitive Slave Act, dramatized slavery's cruelty and its destruction of families. It sold hundreds of thousands of copies, made slavery a moral question for ordinary northern readers, and was banned across the South.
cards.n: It is the standard example of print culture shaping sectional feeling.

cards.q: Identify the Kansas-Nebraska Act and what it repealed.
cards.a: Douglas's 1854 law organized Kansas and Nebraska with slavery decided by popular sovereignty, which explicitly repealed the Missouri Compromise ban on slavery north of 36 degrees 30 minutes. Douglas wanted a northern transcontinental railroad route and southern votes.
cards.n: Repealing a 34-year-old sectional settlement is what made this act so explosive.

cards.q: Explain how the Kansas-Nebraska Act reshaped the party system.
cards.a: It shattered the Whig Party along sectional lines and split northern Democrats. Antislavery Whigs, Free Soilers, and northern Democrats formed the Republican Party in 1854, dedicated to stopping slavery's expansion, creating a purely sectional major party.
cards.h: → which party died, which was born
cards.n: After 1854 no major party had strength in both sections, which is the structural cause of secession in 1860.

cards.q: Identify Bleeding Kansas.
cards.a: The guerrilla warfare of 1855-1858 as proslavery Missouri border ruffians and free-state settlers each set up rival governments. Violence included the sack of Lawrence, John Brown's Pottawatomie Massacre, and the fraudulent proslavery Lecompton Constitution.
cards.n: The caning of Sumner by Preston Brooks in 1856 showed the violence reaching Congress itself.

cards.q: Identify the three holdings of Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857).
cards.a: Chief Justice Taney ruled that Black people were not and could never be citizens and so could not sue; that residence in free territory did not make Scott free; and that Congress could not bar slavery from any territory, making the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional.
cards.n: The third holding logically destroyed both free soil and popular sovereignty, gutting the Republican platform.

cards.q: Explain why Dred Scott intensified rather than settled the sectional crisis.
cards.a: By declaring any federal limit on territorial slavery unconstitutional, the ruling denied the North any legal route to contain slavery and convinced Republicans that a Slave Power conspiracy controlled the government. Republicans campaigned against the decision instead of accepting it.
cards.n: The 14th Amendment's citizenship clause was written specifically to overturn Taney's citizenship holding.

cards.q: Identify the Lincoln-Douglas debates and the Freeport Doctrine.
cards.a: Seven 1858 Illinois Senate debates on slavery in the territories. Douglas argued in the Freeport Doctrine that settlers could exclude slavery in practice by refusing to pass slave codes, which satisfied northerners but alienated southern Democrats.
cards.n: Douglas won the Senate seat but lost the South, splitting the Democrats in 1860 and making Lincoln nationally famous.

cards.q: Identify John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry.
cards.a: In October 1859 Brown and about twenty men seized the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, hoping to arm an uprising of enslaved people. Federal troops crushed the raid and Brown was tried and hanged.
cards.n: Northern intellectuals made him a martyr while the South read that reaction as proof the North endorsed slave insurrection.

cards.q: Identify the four candidates in the election of 1860 and the outcome.
cards.a: Lincoln for the Republicans, Douglas for northern Democrats, Breckinridge for southern Democrats, and Bell for the Constitutional Union Party. Lincoln won a clear electoral majority with under 40 percent of the popular vote and no southern electoral votes.
cards.n: Lincoln was not on the ballot in most southern states, which is why secessionists called his election illegitimate.

cards.q: Explain why Lincoln's election triggered secession even though he promised not to touch slavery where it existed.
cards.a: The result proved the North could elect a president with no southern support, ending the South's national veto. Republicans intended to block slavery's expansion, which secessionists believed would strangle the institution over time and encourage antislavery politics inside the South.
cards.h: → loss of political leverage, not immediate abolition
cards.n: South Carolina's Declaration of Causes says this outright and is a common stimulus document.

cards.q: Date South Carolina's secession, the formation of the Confederacy, and Fort Sumter.
cards.a: South Carolina seceded December 1860; the Confederate States of America formed February 1861; Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861, after which four Upper South states seceded.
cards.n: Only seven states had seceded before Sumter; Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina left after Lincoln called for troops.

cards.q: Explain Lincoln's strategy at Fort Sumter and why it worked politically.
cards.a: Lincoln announced he would resupply the garrison with food only and no weapons, forcing the Confederacy either to accept a federal fort in Charleston harbor or to fire the first shot. The Confederates fired, which unified northern opinion behind the war.
cards.h: → what he sent + the dilemma created
cards.n: He needed the South to be the aggressor to hold the border states and northern Democrats.

cards.q: Contrast Union and Confederate advantages at the start of the Civil War.
cards.a: The Union had roughly four times the free population, most manufacturing, over two-thirds of the railroad mileage, a navy, and an existing government and treasury. The Confederacy had superior officers, interior lines, a defensive war requiring only survival, and expectations of British demand for cotton.
cards.n: King Cotton diplomacy failed because Britain had stockpiles and could turn to Egypt and India.

cards.q: Explain the significance of the Battle of Antietam.
cards.a: Fought in Maryland in September 1862 and the bloodiest single day in American history, it stopped Lee's first invasion of the North. The result discouraged British recognition of the Confederacy and gave Lincoln the victory he needed to issue the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation.
cards.n: A tactical draw that counts as a Union strategic victory because Lee withdrew.

cards.q: Differentiate what the Emancipation Proclamation did from what it did not do.
cards.a: Effective January 1, 1863, it declared enslaved people free in areas still in rebellion and authorized Black enlistment in the Union army. It exempted the loyal border states and Union-occupied areas, so it freed no one the federal government then controlled.
cards.h: → where it applied, where it did not
cards.n: It was a war measure under the president's commander-in-chief power, which is why it could not reach loyal states.

cards.q: Explain the strategic significance of the Emancipation Proclamation.
cards.a: It redefined the war as a fight against slavery, which made British or French intervention politically impossible, drained Confederate labor as enslaved people fled to Union lines, and opened the army to about 180,000 Black soldiers.
cards.n: Black enlistment is the point students most often omit and graders most often reward.

cards.q: Explain why July 1863 is called the turning point of the Civil War.
cards.a: At Gettysburg, Meade repelled Lee's second invasion of the North and the Confederacy never again mounted a major offensive. One day later Vicksburg fell to Grant, giving the Union the Mississippi River and splitting the Confederacy in two.
cards.n: Vicksburg fulfilled a key element of the Anaconda Plan and made Grant's reputation.

cards.q: Identify the Anaconda Plan.
cards.a: Winfield Scott's strategy to strangle the Confederacy by blockading the southern coast, seizing the Mississippi River to cut the South in two, and then squeezing the remaining territory rather than seeking one decisive battle.

cards.q: Identify Sherman's March to the Sea and total war.
cards.a: After taking Atlanta in September 1864, Sherman marched to Savannah and then through the Carolinas, destroying railroads, crops, factories, and civilian property to break the South's capacity and will to fight. It is the standard American example of total war.
cards.n: The fall of Atlanta rescued Lincoln's reelection against McClellan and the peace Democrats.

cards.q: Date Appomattox, Lincoln's assassination, and the 13th Amendment's ratification.
cards.a: Lee surrendered at Appomattox Court House April 9, 1865; Lincoln was assassinated April 14, 1865; the 13th Amendment was ratified in December 1865.
cards.n: Lincoln died five days after Appomattox, leaving Reconstruction to Andrew Johnson.

cards.q: Identify Lincoln's suspension of habeas corpus and the controversy it caused.
cards.a: Lincoln suspended the writ of habeas corpus, beginning in Maryland in 1861, allowing military arrest and detention of suspected Confederate sympathizers without trial. Chief Justice Taney in Ex parte Merryman said only Congress could suspend it; Lincoln ignored the ruling and Congress authorized suspension in 1863.
cards.n: A recurring theme: wartime expansion of executive power, comparable to the Alien and Sedition Acts and later to World War I and II.

cards.q: Identify the New York City draft riots of 1863.
cards.a: Working-class, largely Irish immigrant mobs attacked draft offices, Republican targets, and Black New Yorkers for four days in July 1863, enraged by conscription and the $300 commutation fee that let the wealthy buy exemption.
cards.n: Evidence for the slogan a rich man's war and a poor man's fight; the Confederacy had a parallel twenty-slave exemption.

cards.q: Identify the Homestead Act, the Pacific Railway Act, and the Morrill Land Grant Act.
cards.a: All passed in 1862 by a Congress without southern members. The Homestead Act offered 160 acres free to settlers who farmed it five years; the Pacific Railway Act funded a transcontinental railroad with land grants and loans; the Morrill Act granted public land to fund agricultural and mechanical colleges.
cards.n: These enact the old Whig-Republican program that southern votes had blocked for decades.

cards.q: Explain how Civil War legislation transformed the federal government's role in the economy.
cards.a: Congress created a national banking system and greenback currency, imposed the first income tax, raised protective tariffs, and subsidized railroads, homesteads, and colleges. Federal power over currency, land, and infrastructure expanded permanently.
cards.n: This lays the institutional groundwork for Gilded Age industrial growth in Period 6.

cards.q: State what the 13th Amendment did.
cards.a: Ratified in 1865, it abolished slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States, except as punishment for a crime after conviction.
cards.n: The punishment exception enabled convict leasing in the New South.

cards.q: State what the 14th Amendment did.
cards.a: Ratified in 1868, it granted citizenship to all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and barred states from denying due process or equal protection of the laws. It also reduced representation for states denying male suffrage and barred former Confederate officials from office.
cards.n: It overturned Dred Scott's citizenship holding and is the constitutional basis of twentieth-century civil rights law.

cards.q: State what the 15th Amendment did and what it left out.
cards.a: Ratified in 1870, it barred denying the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude. It said nothing about literacy tests, poll taxes, or sex, leaving the openings later used for disfranchisement.
cards.n: Its silence on sex split the women's suffrage movement into the NWSA and AWSA.

cards.q: Date the ratification of the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments.
cards.a: 13th Amendment 1865; 14th Amendment 1868; 15th Amendment 1870.

cards.q: Contrast Lincoln's Ten Percent Plan with the Wade-Davis Bill.
cards.a: Lincoln's 1863 plan readmitted a state once ten percent of its 1860 voters swore loyalty and accepted emancipation. The 1864 Wade-Davis Bill required a majority to take an ironclad oath and demanded stronger guarantees; Lincoln pocket-vetoed it.
cards.n: The clash establishes the presidential-versus-congressional control fight that dominates Reconstruction.

cards.q: Contrast Presidential Reconstruction under Johnson with Radical Reconstruction under Congress.
cards.a: Johnson required only loyalty oaths, the 13th Amendment, and repudiation of Confederate debt, pardoned planters freely, and left freedpeople's rights to the states. Congress from 1867 imposed military rule, required the 14th Amendment and Black male suffrage, and used federal power to protect freedpeople.
cards.n: Johnson's leniency and the black codes are what provoked congressional takeover.

cards.q: Identify the Freedmen's Bureau.
cards.a: A federal agency created in 1865 to aid formerly enslaved people and poor whites with food, medical care, legal help, labor contract supervision, and above all schools. It founded thousands of schools and several Black colleges before Congress ended it in 1872.
cards.n: It is the first major federal social welfare agency; Johnson vetoed its expansion.

cards.q: Identify the black codes.
cards.a: Laws passed by southern states in 1865-1866 restricting freedpeople through vagrancy statutes that forced them into labor contracts, apprenticeship laws seizing children, bans on renting land, and limits on court testimony, gun ownership, and movement.
cards.n: They recreated slavery's labor control without owning people, which is precisely why Congress passed the 14th Amendment.

cards.q: Define sharecropping.
cards.a: A postwar labor system in which a landowner supplied land, tools, seed, and housing while a family farmed and paid a share of the crop, usually one-third to one-half, as rent. It replaced gang labor with family-based tenancy.
cards.h: → who supplies what, who pays what
cards.n: It was a compromise: planters wanted wage gangs, freedpeople wanted land, and neither got it.

cards.q: Explain how sharecropping and the crop-lien system trapped families in debt.
cards.a: Sharecroppers bought supplies on credit from merchants at high interest, pledging the coming crop as collateral. Cotton prices fell through the late 1800s, so the crop rarely covered the debt, and laws let creditors hold families in place year after year.
cards.n: This economic dependency is why emancipation did not deliver economic freedom, a common continuity argument.

cards.q: Identify the Reconstruction Acts of 1867.
cards.a: They divided the ten unreconstructed southern states into five military districts under army commanders, required new constitutional conventions elected with Black male participation, and made readmission conditional on ratifying the 14th Amendment and guaranteeing Black male suffrage.
cards.n: This is the start of Radical or Congressional Reconstruction proper.

cards.q: Identify the impeachment of Andrew Johnson.
cards.a: The House impeached Johnson in 1868 for removing Secretary of War Stanton in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act, part of his broader obstruction of Reconstruction. The Senate acquitted him by a single vote.
cards.n: Senators who acquitted feared that removing a president over policy disagreement would unbalance the branches.

cards.q: Identify the extent of Black political participation during Reconstruction.
cards.a: Roughly 2,000 Black men held office, including sixteen in Congress and senators Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce of Mississippi. Black voters and legislators helped write new state constitutions creating public schools and expanding civil rights.
cards.n: This directly refutes the discredited Dunning School portrait of Reconstruction governments as incompetent.

cards.q: Differentiate carpetbaggers from scalawags.
cards.a: Southern Democrats' insults for their opponents: carpetbaggers were northerners who moved south after the war, and scalawags were white southerners who cooperated with Republicans, often upcountry yeomen and former Whigs.
cards.n: Both terms come from hostile propaganda, so sourcing questions often ask about their point of view.

cards.q: Identify the Ku Klux Klan and the federal response.
cards.a: A secret terrorist organization formed in 1866 that used murder, whipping, and arson to intimidate Black voters, officeholders, and white Republicans. Congress answered with the Enforcement Acts of 1870-1871, including the Ku Klux Klan Act, letting federal courts and troops prosecute conspiracies.
cards.n: The Enforcement Acts worked briefly, which shows that Reconstruction failed from lost political will, not from lack of tools.

cards.q: Identify the holding of the Slaughterhouse Cases (1873).
cards.a: The Court read the 14th Amendment's privileges or immunities clause narrowly, holding it protected only the few rights of national citizenship and left most civil rights under state control, sharply limiting federal protection of individual rights.
cards.n: The first major judicial retreat from Reconstruction; pair it with the Civil Rights Cases and Plessy.

cards.q: Identify the holding of the Civil Rights Cases (1883).
cards.a: The Court struck down the Civil Rights Act of 1875, ruling that the 14th Amendment reaches only state action and not discrimination by private individuals or businesses such as inns, theaters, and railroads.
cards.n: The state action doctrine left private segregation untouched until the Civil Rights Act of 1964 used the commerce clause instead. Note the periodization: 1883 falls in Period 6 (1865-1898) even though this card sits with the Period 5 Reconstruction material.

cards.q: Identify the Compromise of 1877.
cards.a: The deal resolving the disputed Hayes-Tilden election: Democrats accepted Republican Rutherford B. Hayes as president in exchange for the withdrawal of remaining federal troops from the South, effectively ending Reconstruction.
cards.h: → who got the presidency, who got what
cards.n: Troops did not literally leave the South; they stopped propping up Republican state governments.

cards.q: Explain why Reconstruction ended.
cards.a: Northern voters tired of intervention and turned to the Panic of 1873 and Grant-era corruption scandals; the Supreme Court narrowed the Reconstruction amendments; white Democratic redeemers regained southern statehouses through violence and fraud; and the Compromise of 1877 removed federal enforcement.
cards.h: → four causes: opinion, courts, violence, politics
cards.n: Best answers weigh multiple causes rather than blaming 1877 alone.

cards.q: Differentiate what Reconstruction achieved from what it failed to achieve.
cards.a: It achieved the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments, Black officeholding, Black churches and schools, and public education in the South. It failed to deliver land redistribution, lasting voting rights, economic independence, or protection from terror once federal enforcement ended.
cards.n: Foner's framing of an unfinished revolution is the standard historiographical line for this prompt.

cards.q: Define the Gilded Age.
cards.a: The label from Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner's 1873 novel for the era from about 1870 to 1900: a thin gilding of spectacular wealth and industrial growth over corruption, political machines, and severe inequality.
cards.h: → origin of the term + what it implies
cards.n: Gilded means covered in gold leaf, not golden; the whole point is the contrast between surface and substance.

cards.q: Identify the transcontinental railroad and how it was built.
cards.a: The Union Pacific building west and the Central Pacific building east met at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869. Federal land grants and loans funded it, and the labor came largely from Chinese immigrants in the West and Irish immigrants and veterans in the East.
cards.h: → two companies, meeting point, labor force
cards.n: Government subsidy of private corporations is the standard illustration that laissez-faire was never absolute.

cards.q: Date the completion of the first transcontinental railroad and the Interstate Commerce Act.
cards.a: Transcontinental railroad completed 1869; Interstate Commerce Act passed 1887.

cards.q: Explain how railroads transformed the national economy.
cards.a: They created a genuinely national market for mass-produced goods, drove demand for steel and coal, opened western land to settlement and cattle, standardized time zones in 1883, and pioneered modern corporate management with professional managers and vast capital from stock markets.
cards.n: Railroads were the first big business and the model for corporate organization everywhere else.

cards.q: Identify Andrew Carnegie's role in industrialization.
cards.a: Carnegie built a steel empire around the Bessemer process and vertical integration, owning ore, coal, ships, and railroads to control costs. He sold Carnegie Steel to J.P. Morgan in 1901 for the U.S. Steel merger and gave away most of his fortune to libraries and universities.
cards.n: Pair Carnegie with vertical integration and the Gospel of Wealth on comparison questions.

cards.q: Identify John D. Rockefeller's role in industrialization.
cards.a: Rockefeller built Standard Oil through horizontal integration, buying or destroying rivals with secret railroad rebates and price cutting until he refined about 90 percent of American oil, then organized the trust form to hold the combination together.
cards.n: Ida Tarbell's exposure of Standard Oil later becomes a founding text of muckraking in Period 7.

cards.q: Identify J.P. Morgan's role in industrialization.
cards.a: Morgan was an investment banker who consolidated railroads and industries, placing his own men on boards, and in 1901 combined Carnegie Steel and rivals into U.S. Steel, the first billion-dollar corporation. He twice lent gold to rescue the federal Treasury.
cards.n: Morgan represents finance capitalism, distinct from Carnegie and Rockefeller as producers.

cards.q: Contrast vertical and horizontal integration.
cards.a: Vertical integration means owning every stage from raw materials through transport to sales, as Carnegie did in steel, to cut costs and escape suppliers. Horizontal integration means absorbing competitors at the same stage, as Rockefeller did in refining, to control prices and end competition.
cards.h: → up-and-down the chain vs across the same stage
cards.n: A high-frequency multiple-choice distinction; anchor each to its industrialist.

cards.q: Define a trust as used in the late nineteenth century.
cards.a: A legal arrangement in which stockholders of competing companies transferred their shares to a single board of trustees, which then ran all the firms as one, allowing monopoly control while keeping the companies nominally separate.
cards.n: When states outlawed trusts, firms shifted to holding companies chartered in permissive states like New Jersey.

cards.q: Define Social Darwinism.
cards.a: The application of survival of the fittest to society, associated with Herbert Spencer and William Graham Sumner, arguing that wealth proves fitness, poverty proves unfitness, and government aid to the poor interferes with natural progress.
cards.n: It supplied the moral defense of laissez-faire and later of immigration restriction and imperialism.

cards.q: Identify Carnegie's Gospel of Wealth.
cards.a: Carnegie's 1889 essay arguing that concentration of wealth is natural and beneficial, but that the rich hold their fortunes as trustees for society and should give them away during their lifetimes to libraries, schools, and other institutions that help people help themselves.
cards.h: → wealth is fine, but with what duty
cards.n: It endorses charity for self-improvement, not direct relief, which Carnegie thought harmful.

cards.q: Contrast Social Darwinism with the Gospel of Wealth and the Social Gospel.
cards.a: Social Darwinism says the poor deserve their fate and deserve no help. The Gospel of Wealth accepts inequality but obligates the rich to fund uplift institutions. The Social Gospel, preached by Walter Rauschenbusch, says Christianity requires attacking poverty's structural causes through reform.
cards.h: → three positions on obligation to the poor
cards.n: The Social Gospel feeds directly into settlement houses and Progressivism.

cards.q: Define laissez-faire and explain how consistently it was practiced.
cards.a: The doctrine that government should not regulate the economy. In practice government intervened constantly on business's side through protective tariffs, railroad land grants, hard money policy, and troops or injunctions used to break strikes.
cards.n: The strongest essays note that laissez-faire was applied selectively, never to subsidies.

cards.q: Identify the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 and its early record.
cards.a: It outlawed combinations in restraint of trade, but its vague wording and hostile courts made it nearly useless against corporations. In United States v. E. C. Knight (1895) the Court exempted manufacturing from interstate commerce, gutting the law.
cards.h: → what it banned + why it failed
cards.n: Before 1900 it was used more successfully against labor unions than against trusts.

cards.q: Explain how the Sherman Antitrust Act was turned against labor unions.
cards.a: Courts held that strikes and boycotts were conspiracies in restraint of interstate trade, so federal judges issued injunctions ordering strikers back to work. The Pullman Strike injunction of 1894 was upheld in In re Debs, jailing Eugene Debs.
cards.h: → strike as restraint of trade + the remedy
cards.n: A textbook irony question: a law aimed at trusts became a weapon against workers.

cards.q: Identify the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887.
cards.a: Prompted by farmer protest and by Wabash v. Illinois (1886), which barred states from regulating interstate rates, it required reasonable and just railroad rates, banned rebates and pooling, and created the Interstate Commerce Commission, the first federal regulatory agency.
cards.h: → trigger case + what agency it created
cards.n: The ICC had weak enforcement and lost most early court cases, but it set the precedent for federal regulation.

cards.q: Contrast the holdings of Munn v. Illinois and Wabash v. Illinois.
cards.a: Munn v. Illinois (1877) upheld state regulation of grain elevators and railroads as businesses clothed with a public interest, validating Granger laws. Wabash v. Illinois (1886) reversed course, holding that only Congress may regulate interstate rates.
cards.h: → one allows state power, one removes it
cards.n: Wabash is the direct cause of the Interstate Commerce Act one year later.

cards.q: Identify the Knights of Labor.
cards.a: A broad union led by Terence Powderly that after 1879 admitted skilled and unskilled workers, women, and Black workers, seeking the eight-hour day, an end to child labor, and producer cooperatives rather than the wage system. Membership collapsed after Haymarket in 1886.
cards.n: It preferred arbitration to strikes, yet was destroyed by public association with anarchist violence.

cards.q: Identify the American Federation of Labor and Samuel Gompers.
cards.a: Founded in 1886, the AFL was a federation of craft unions of skilled workers led by Gompers. It practiced bread-and-butter unionism, bargaining for higher wages, shorter hours, and better conditions rather than remaking society, and it used strikes and boycotts.
cards.n: By excluding unskilled workers, most women, and most Black workers, the AFL survived but represented a small slice of labor.

cards.q: Contrast the Knights of Labor with the American Federation of Labor.
cards.a: The Knights were inclusive of nearly all workers and pursued broad social reform and cooperatives. The AFL organized only skilled craft workers and pursued concrete workplace gains within capitalism. The inclusive model collapsed; the narrow model endured.
cards.n: The tradeoff between inclusiveness and effectiveness is the point graders look for.

cards.q: Identify the Great Railroad Strike of 1877.
cards.a: After repeated wage cuts during the depression following the Panic of 1873, railroad workers struck across the country, halting much of the rail system. President Hayes sent federal troops to break the strike, and about 100 people died.
cards.n: The first nationwide strike and the first use of federal troops against strikers in peacetime.

cards.q: Identify the Haymarket affair.
cards.a: At a Chicago rally in May 1886 supporting the eight-hour day, a bomb killed police officers and gunfire followed. Eight anarchists were convicted on scant evidence and four were hanged, and the episode linked unions with foreign radicalism in the public mind.
cards.n: It destroyed the Knights of Labor and fused anti-union feeling with anti-immigrant fear.

cards.q: Identify the Homestead Strike of 1892.
cards.a: At Carnegie's Homestead steel plant near Pittsburgh, manager Henry Clay Frick cut wages and locked out the union, then hired 300 Pinkerton guards. A gun battle killed people on both sides, the state militia occupied the town, and the union was destroyed.
cards.n: Carnegie was in Scotland; his absence while Frick crushed the union is a standard sourcing wrinkle.

cards.q: Identify the Pullman Strike of 1894.
cards.a: Pullman cut wages in his company town without cutting rents, so workers struck and Eugene Debs's American Railway Union boycotted Pullman cars nationally. Attorney General Olney obtained a federal injunction on the grounds of obstructing the mail, and Cleveland sent troops.
cards.n: The court injunction became the employers' most effective anti-strike weapon until the 1930s.

cards.q: Date the four major Gilded Age labor conflicts in order.
cards.a: Great Railroad Strike 1877; Haymarket affair 1886; Homestead Strike 1892; Pullman Strike 1894.
cards.n: 1886 also gives the AFL's founding and the eight-hour-day campaign.

cards.q: Explain why organized labor achieved so little in the Gilded Age.
cards.a: Employers used lockouts, blacklists, yellow-dog contracts, private guards, and strikebreakers; courts issued injunctions and treated unions as conspiracies; government sent troops; and workers were divided by skill, ethnicity, race, and gender while immigration kept replacement labor plentiful.
cards.h: → employer, court, state, and internal weaknesses
cards.n: Union membership stayed under about 5 percent of the workforce through the era.

cards.q: Define the new immigration of the late nineteenth century.
cards.a: The shift after about 1880 toward immigrants from southern and eastern Europe, especially Italians, Poles, Slavs, Greeks, and Jews from Russia and Austria-Hungary, who were largely Catholic or Jewish, poor, and settled in industrial cities.
cards.n: Contrast with old immigration from Britain, Ireland, Germany, and Scandinavia before 1880.

cards.q: Contrast old and new immigration in origin, religion, and reception.
cards.a: Old immigrants came from northern and western Europe, were mostly Protestant apart from the Irish, and often moved to farms. New immigrants came from southern and eastern Europe, were mostly Catholic, Orthodox, or Jewish, crowded into urban tenements, and faced sharper nativist hostility and calls for literacy tests.
cards.n: This comparison sets up the 1920s national origins quotas in Period 7.

cards.q: Contrast the immigrant experience at Ellis Island with that at Angel Island.
cards.a: Ellis Island opened in New York Harbor in 1892 to process European arrivals, most of whom cleared inspection in hours. Angel Island opened in San Francisco Bay in 1910 and detained Asian arrivals, especially Chinese, for weeks or months of interrogation.
cards.n: The contrast in treatment is the point: European entry was fast, Asian entry was obstructed.

cards.q: Identify the Chinese Exclusion Act.
cards.a: The 1882 law barring Chinese laborers from immigrating and denying Chinese immigrants naturalization, driven by west coast labor competition and racial hostility. It was the first U.S. law to exclude a group by nationality and was renewed until 1943.
cards.h: → who was barred + its historical first
cards.n: It shows federal power turned to racial exclusion at the same moment Reconstruction protections were collapsing.

cards.q: Date the Chinese Exclusion Act, the opening of Ellis Island, and the founding of Hull House.
cards.a: Chinese Exclusion Act 1882; Hull House founded 1889; Ellis Island opened 1892.

cards.q: Explain how industrial growth reshaped the physical layout of American cities.
cards.a: Steel-frame skyscrapers and elevators pushed cities upward; electric streetcars and elevated lines let the middle class move to suburbs; and the poor packed into dumbbell tenements with little light, air, or sanitation, producing sharply segregated cities by class and ethnicity.
cards.n: Jacob Riis's How the Other Half Lives (1890) documented tenement conditions with photographs.

cards.q: Identify political machines and Tammany Hall.
cards.a: Urban party organizations that traded jobs, food, coal, and help with police or landlords for immigrant votes, financing it with kickbacks and graft. New York's Tammany Hall under Boss Tweed stole tens of millions through padded contracts before Tweed's fall in the 1870s.
cards.n: Thomas Nast's cartoons brought Tweed down and are common stimulus images.

cards.q: Explain why political machines were so durable despite their corruption.
cards.a: They delivered services no one else provided: jobs, emergency relief, naturalization help, and a personal contact in government for immigrants ignored by formal institutions. Voters traded a tolerance for graft for tangible aid.
cards.n: Machines are a good counter to the assumption that Gilded Age government did nothing for the poor.

cards.q: Identify the settlement house movement and Jane Addams.
cards.a: Settlement houses were community centers in poor immigrant neighborhoods staffed by educated, mostly female reformers who lived on site and offered kindergartens, English classes, health services, and job training. Addams founded Hull House in Chicago in 1889.
cards.n: Settlement work opened public careers for college-educated women and fed directly into Progressivism.

cards.q: Identify the Pendleton Civil Service Act.
cards.a: Passed in 1883 after Garfield's assassination by a disappointed office seeker, it created the Civil Service Commission and required competitive exams for a growing share of federal jobs, replacing patronage with merit hiring.
cards.n: It pushed parties toward corporate donors for funding once they lost patronage money.

cards.q: Explain the economic grievances of late-nineteenth-century farmers.
cards.a: Overproduction and world competition drove crop prices down for decades while deflation raised the real value of mortgage debt. Railroads charged high monopoly rates at local shipping points, middlemen took a cut, and tariffs kept manufactured goods expensive.
cards.n: Deflation is the key mechanism: farmers repaid fixed debts with dollars that grew more valuable each year.

cards.q: Identify the Farmers' Alliance and the Grange.
cards.a: The Grange, founded in 1867, organized farmers socially and pushed state Granger laws regulating railroads and grain elevators. The Farmers' Alliance of the 1880s built cooperatives and a subtreasury plan for crop-backed federal loans, and became the base for the Populist Party.
cards.n: The Colored Farmers' Alliance organized over a million Black farmers, an interracial opening white Democrats worked to close.

cards.q: Identify the Populist Party and the Omaha Platform.
cards.a: The People's Party formed in 1892 and its Omaha Platform demanded free and unlimited coinage of silver at 16 to 1, a graduated income tax, government ownership of railroads and telegraphs, the subtreasury plan, direct election of senators, the secret ballot, and an eight-hour day.
cards.n: Most Omaha demands became law in the Progressive Era or the New Deal, which is the standard significance point.

cards.q: Define free silver and explain who wanted it.
cards.a: The demand that the Treasury coin unlimited silver at a 16 to 1 ratio to gold, expanding the money supply. Debtor farmers and silver miners wanted the resulting inflation to raise crop prices and ease debts; creditors, bankers, and eastern business defended the gold standard.
cards.n: Money supply is the central political issue of the 1890s and the reason the 1896 election mattered.

cards.q: Identify William Jennings Bryan and the Cross of Gold speech.
cards.a: At the 1896 Democratic convention Bryan demanded free silver, warning that the gold standard crucified mankind upon a cross of gold. The speech won him the Democratic nomination at age 36, and the Populists also endorsed him.
cards.n: Fusion with the Democrats effectively ended the Populist Party as an independent force.

cards.q: Identify the outcome of the election of 1896.
cards.a: Republican William McKinley, funded lavishly by Mark Hanna and business, ran a front-porch campaign for the gold standard, high tariffs, and prosperity, and defeated Bryan by carrying the industrial Northeast and Midwest including urban workers.
cards.n: Bryan's rural evangelical appeal repelled the urban wage earners he needed.

cards.q: Explain the significance of the election of 1896.
cards.a: It ended the era of narrowly divided parties and began roughly a generation of Republican dominance, settled the money question in favor of the gold standard, absorbed Populism into the Democratic Party, and shifted politics from sectional loyalty to urban-industrial versus rural interests.
cards.n: Often called the first modern presidential campaign for its money and organization.

cards.q: Date the founding of the Grange, the Omaha Platform, and the election of 1896.
cards.a: Grange founded 1867; Populist Omaha Platform 1892; Bryan's Cross of Gold speech and McKinley's victory 1896.
cards.n: The Panic of 1893 falls between the Omaha Platform and 1896 and radicalized the debate.

cards.q: Identify the Dawes Severalty Act.
cards.a: The 1887 law that broke up tribal landholding by allotting 160-acre parcels to individual Native heads of household, held in trust for 25 years, offering citizenship to allottees who accepted, and selling surplus land to white settlers.
cards.h: → mechanism + what happened to the surplus
cards.n: It attacked communal landholding deliberately, because reformers believed private property would force assimilation.

cards.q: Explain the intent and the actual effect of the Dawes Act.
cards.a: Reformers intended to assimilate Native people into individual farming and citizenship, supported by boarding schools such as Carlisle that aimed to kill the Indian and save the man. In practice Native landholding fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to about 48 million by 1934.
cards.n: The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 finally reversed allotment.

cards.q: Identify the Ghost Dance movement and the massacre at Wounded Knee.
cards.a: The Ghost Dance was a religious revival promising the return of the buffalo and ancestors and the disappearance of white settlers. Alarmed agents suppressed it; Sitting Bull was killed during an arrest, and in December 1890 the Seventh Cavalry killed roughly 250 to 300 Lakota at Wounded Knee, South Dakota.
cards.n: Conventionally marks the end of armed Native resistance on the Plains.

cards.q: Identify Frederick Jackson Turner's Frontier Thesis.
cards.a: Turner argued in 1893 that the frontier experience of settling free land had shaped American democracy, individualism, and innovation, and that the Census declaration of a closed frontier in 1890 meant a defining era of American development had ended.
cards.n: Historians criticize it for ignoring Native peoples, women, and the federal role, and for treating the West as empty.

cards.q: Date the Dawes Act, Wounded Knee, and Turner's Frontier Thesis.
cards.a: Dawes Severalty Act 1887; Wounded Knee massacre 1890; Turner's Frontier Thesis presented 1893.
cards.n: The Census announcement of a closed frontier in 1890 sits between the massacre and Turner's essay.

cards.q: Differentiate New South rhetoric from southern economic reality after 1877.
cards.a: Henry Grady's program for a diversified, industrialized, self-sufficient South with textile mills, tobacco, iron, and railroads. Some industry did grow, but the region stayed poor and agricultural, sharecropping and cotton dependence persisted, and racial hierarchy hardened.
cards.n: A favorite continuity-and-change prompt: rhetoric of change over substantial continuity.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896).
cards.a: The Court upheld a Louisiana railroad segregation law, ruling that separate accommodations do not violate the 14th Amendment's equal protection clause so long as they are equal. Justice Harlan dissented that the Constitution is color-blind.
cards.h: → the doctrine it created + the lone dissent
cards.n: Separate but equal governed until Brown v. Board in 1954; facilities were never actually equal.

cards.q: Define Jim Crow.
cards.a: The system of state and local laws and customs from the 1880s onward that segregated southern schools, transport, restaurants, hospitals, and public spaces by race, enforced by legal penalties and by extralegal violence including lynching.
cards.n: Jim Crow segregation is a post-Reconstruction creation, not a holdover from slavery.

cards.q: Identify the methods southern states used to disfranchise Black voters without violating the 15th Amendment.
cards.a: Poll taxes, literacy and understanding tests administered by white registrars, residency requirements, all-white primaries, and grandfather clauses exempting men whose grandfathers had voted before 1867. All were race-neutral on their face.
cards.n: Facial neutrality is the whole trick; the 15th Amendment banned explicit racial tests only.

cards.q: Identify Booker T. Washington and the Atlanta Compromise.
cards.a: Founder of Tuskegee Institute, Washington argued in his 1895 Atlanta Exposition address that Black Americans should accept segregation for the moment and build economic strength through vocational and industrial training, saying the races could be as separate as the fingers in social matters.
cards.n: White philanthropists and politicians made him the most powerful Black leader of his era, which is part of why Du Bois objected.

cards.q: Contrast Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois.
cards.a: Washington urged accommodation, vocational training, and gradual economic uplift before pressing for rights. Du Bois, in The Souls of Black Folk (1903), demanded immediate civil and political rights, liberal arts education, and leadership by a Talented Tenth, and he helped found the Niagara Movement and the NAACP.
cards.n: The highest-frequency comparison question in Periods 6 and 7; both sought equality, differing on means and pace.

cards.q: Identify Ida B. Wells and her anti-lynching campaign.
cards.a: A Memphis journalist who investigated lynchings after friends were murdered in 1892, publishing statistics showing that lynching punished Black economic success and disproved the rape accusations used to justify it. Her press was destroyed and she carried the campaign north and to Britain.
cards.h: → method of argument + what she disproved
cards.n: Her use of data and eyewitness evidence prefigures muckraking journalism.

cards.q: Differentiate the position of Black southerners in 1870 from their position in 1900.
cards.a: In 1870 Black men voted in large numbers, held office, and had federal protection under the Reconstruction amendments. By 1900 disfranchisement, Jim Crow laws, Plessy, sharecropping debt, and lynching had stripped political power and economic mobility while the amendments remained on the books unenforced.
cards.h: → then vs now on rights, economy, safety
cards.n: The gap between formal constitutional rights and lived reality is the through-line into Period 8.

cards.q: Explain why Gilded Age national politics accomplished so little.
cards.a: Elections were extremely close with divided control of Congress and one-term presidents, both parties served business interests and differed mainly on tariffs and patronage, voter loyalty ran on Civil War memory and ethnicity rather than policy, and laissez-faire ideology discouraged federal action.
cards.n: The vacuum at the national level is why reform first appeared in states, cities, and third parties.

cards.q: Differentiate Populism from the Progressivism that followed it.
cards.a: Populism was rural, southern and western, agrarian, and rooted in producer grievances, demanding inflation and government ownership. Progressivism was urban, middle-class, and professional, seeking expert regulation, efficiency, and moral reform of business and politics rather than farmer relief.
cards.n: Many Omaha Platform demands were later enacted by Progressives, which is the connection to draw.

cards.q: Define muckrakers and name several of them with their targets.
cards.a: Investigative journalists of the early 1900s who exposed corruption and abuse to spur reform. Upton Sinclair (meatpacking, The Jungle), Ida Tarbell (Standard Oil), Jacob Riis (tenement poverty, How the Other Half Lives), Lincoln Steffens (city machines).
cards.n: Muckrakers are the classic DBQ example of press pressure producing federal regulation.

cards.q: Identify the two 1906 laws that followed publication of The Jungle.
cards.a: The Pure Food and Drug Act (banned mislabeled and adulterated food and medicine, basis of the FDA) and the Meat Inspection Act (federal inspection of meatpacking plants).
cards.n: Sinclair aimed at workers and hit consumers instead: he said he aimed at the public's heart and hit its stomach.

cards.q: Define Theodore Roosevelt's Square Deal and list its three C's.
cards.a: TR's domestic program promising fairness to labor, business, and consumers. The three C's: control of corporations (trust-busting bad trusts), consumer protection, and conservation of natural resources.
cards.n: TR distinguished good trusts from bad trusts; he regulated far more than he broke up.
x: control of corporations, consumer protection, conservation

cards.q: Name the direct-democracy reforms Progressives used to weaken party machines.
cards.a: The initiative (voters propose laws), the referendum (voters approve or reject laws), the recall (voters remove officials), the secret ballot, direct primaries, and the direct election of senators.
cards.n: Pioneered at the state level, especially Wisconsin under Robert La Follette (the Wisconsin Idea).

cards.q: Identify the Federal Reserve Act (1913) and its purpose.
cards.a: Wilson-era law creating a central banking system of twelve regional Federal Reserve banks under a national board, empowered to set interest rates and issue currency to stabilize the money supply and prevent panics.
cards.n: The most durable New Freedom reform; it answers the long Populist demand for a flexible currency.

cards.q: Identify the Clayton Antitrust Act (1914).
cards.a: It strengthened the Sherman Act by banning price discrimination and interlocking directorates, and exempted labor unions and farm organizations from antitrust prosecution, legalizing strikes, boycotts, and peaceful picketing.
cards.n: Samuel Gompers called it labor's Magna Carta, though the courts later narrowed the exemption.

cards.q: Identify the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire and its consequence.
cards.a: A 1911 New York factory fire that killed 146 workers, mostly young immigrant women, who were trapped behind locked exit doors. It produced state fire-safety codes, factory inspection laws, and stronger workers' compensation rules.
cards.n: Prime evidence that much Progressive labor reform happened at the state, not the federal, level.

cards.q: State what the 16th Amendment (1913) established.
cards.a: It authorized Congress to levy a federal income tax without apportioning it among the states by population.
cards.n: The income tax made a large federal state financially possible, from the New Deal to WWII mobilization.

cards.q: State what the 17th Amendment (1913) changed.
cards.a: It provided for the direct popular election of U.S. senators, who had previously been chosen by state legislatures.
cards.n: Textbook Progressive answer to machine politics and to a Senate mocked as the millionaires' club.

cards.q: State what the 18th Amendment (1919) did and what enforced it.
cards.a: It prohibited the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors nationwide. The Volstead Act supplied the enforcement machinery. The 21st Amendment repealed it in 1933.
cards.n: Prohibition bridges Progressive moral reform and 1920s cultural conflict, and it fed organized crime.

cards.q: State what the 19th Amendment (1920) guaranteed.
cards.a: It barred the states and the federal government from denying the right to vote on account of sex, granting women nationwide suffrage.
cards.n: Capstone of a movement running from Seneca Falls in 1848; wartime service gave the final push.

cards.q: Define yellow journalism and name its two leading practitioners.
cards.a: Sensational, exaggerated reporting designed to sell newspapers. William Randolph Hearst (New York Journal) and Joseph Pulitzer (New York World) inflamed public anger over Spanish rule in Cuba before 1898.
cards.n: Classic sourcing question: yellow-press coverage shows how purpose and audience shape evidence.

cards.q: Identify the Teller Amendment and the Platt Amendment.
cards.a: The Teller Amendment (1898) pledged that the U.S. would not annex Cuba. The Platt Amendment (1901) then forced Cuba to permit U.S. intervention, to limit its treaty-making and debt, and to lease Guantanamo Bay to the United States.
cards.n: The pair is the sharpest evidence of the gap between anti-imperialist rhetoric and imperial practice.

cards.q: Identify the Philippine-American War and the Anti-Imperialist League.
cards.a: After annexation in 1898, Emilio Aguinaldo's forces fought a brutal U.S. counterinsurgency (1899-1902) that killed hundreds of thousands of Filipinos. The Anti-Imperialist League (Twain, Carnegie, Bryan, Addams) opposed annexation as a betrayal of self-government.
cards.n: Shows that empire was contested at home; the war undercut the civilizing-mission justification.

cards.q: Define the Open Door Policy.
cards.a: Secretary of State John Hay's 1899-1900 notes asking the imperial powers to keep equal trading access to all of China and to preserve Chinese territorial integrity, protecting U.S. commercial opportunity without colonies.
cards.n: The economic model of U.S. expansion: markets and access rather than territory.

cards.q: State the Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine (1904).
cards.a: TR asserted that chronic wrongdoing or instability in Latin America could compel the United States to act as an international police power, intervening to preempt European debt collection in the hemisphere.
cards.n: It turns Monroe's defensive warning into a claimed right to intervene; cite it for Big Stick diplomacy.

cards.q: Identify the Zimmermann Telegram.
cards.a: A secret 1917 German message, intercepted by the British, offering Mexico an alliance and the recovery of Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona if the U.S. entered the war. Its publication enraged American opinion.
cards.n: Combined with unrestricted submarine warfare, it is the standard proximate cause of U.S. entry.

cards.q: Identify the Espionage Act (1917) and the Sedition Act (1918).
cards.a: Wartime laws criminalizing interference with the draft or military operations (Espionage) and disloyal, profane, or abusive speech about the government, flag, or armed forces (Sedition). Socialist Eugene Debs was imprisoned under them.
cards.n: The best evidence for wartime contraction of civil liberties; pair them with Schenck.

cards.q: Identify Schenck v. United States (1919) and its legal test.
cards.a: The Supreme Court unanimously upheld an Espionage Act conviction for anti-draft leaflets. Justice Holmes held that speech creating a clear and present danger of substantive evils Congress may prevent is unprotected, especially in wartime.
cards.n: Holmes's falsely shouting fire in a theater line comes from this case; the test stood until Brandenburg (1969).

cards.q: Identify the Committee on Public Information.
cards.a: The federal propaganda agency under George Creel that mobilized opinion for WWI through posters, films, press releases, and Four Minute Men speakers, promoting patriotism and anti-German sentiment.
cards.n: It fed the wave of anti-German hysteria and pressure for conformity on the home front.

cards.q: Define the Great Migration.
cards.a: The movement of roughly one and a half million African Americans out of the rural South to Northern and Midwestern cities from about 1910 to 1940, driven by wartime industrial jobs, boll weevil crop failures, and escape from Jim Crow and lynching.
cards.n: Push-pull migration card: it reshaped Northern politics, produced the Harlem Renaissance, and sparked race riots.

cards.q: State the purpose and key elements of Wilson's Fourteen Points.
cards.a: Wilson's 1918 peace program: open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, free trade, arms reduction, national self-determination, adjustment of colonial claims, and above all Point 14, a general association of nations, the League.
cards.n: Only self-determination and the League survived at Versailles; the rest lost out to Allied demands for reparations.

cards.q: Define the First Red Scare and identify the Palmer Raids.
cards.a: The 1919-1920 panic over communism, anarchism, and labor radicalism after the Bolshevik Revolution and a wave of strikes and bombings. Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer's raids arrested thousands of suspected radicals and deported hundreds without due process.
cards.n: Sacco and Vanzetti's 1921 trial and 1927 execution is the standard illustration of nativist and anti-radical bias.

cards.q: Identify the Emergency Quota Act (1921) and the National Origins Act (1924).
cards.a: Immigration laws that imposed national-origins quotas pegged to earlier census counts, sharply restricting southern and eastern Europeans, and barring most Asian immigration entirely. Western Hemisphere migration was left unrestricted.
cards.n: The 1924 quotas used the 1890 census on purpose, to favor northern and western Europeans; repealed in 1965.

cards.q: Identify the Scopes Trial (1925) and what it symbolized.
cards.a: The Tennessee prosecution of teacher John Scopes for teaching evolution. William Jennings Bryan argued for the state and Clarence Darrow for the defense. Scopes was convicted, but the trial dramatized the clash between fundamentalism and modern science.
cards.n: Use it as evidence of the urban-rural, modernist-fundamentalist divide of the 1920s.

cards.q: Define the Harlem Renaissance and name several figures.
cards.a: The 1920s flowering of African American literature, art, and music centered in Harlem, asserting racial pride and a distinct Black cultural identity. Figures: Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Claude McKay, Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong.
cards.n: Direct product of the Great Migration; connect culture to demographic change on the exam.

cards.q: Define the Lost Generation.
cards.a: Postwar American writers disillusioned by WWI and by 1920s materialism and conformity, many of them expatriates in Paris. Key figures: Ernest Hemingway, F. Scott Fitzgerald, Gertrude Stein, T.S. Eliot.
cards.n: Cultural evidence that WWI shattered Progressive confidence in reform and progress.

cards.q: Define 1920s consumer culture and the credit practice that fueled it.
cards.a: Mass production (Ford's assembly line), national advertising, radio, and chain stores created a market for cars, appliances, and radios. Installment buying let consumers purchase on credit, sustaining demand but building household debt.
cards.n: Buying on the installment plan and stock buying on margin are the two debt habits that made 1929 worse.
